title: Here’s What 2 Weeks of Vacation Taught Me About Leadership
author: The Good Boss
summary: The author, a technology leader, recounts finally disconnecting for two full weeks after years of checking email in vacation queues. He returns expecting an avalanche of problems and instead finds a team that made decisions, handled customer escalations and ran a blameless postmortem without him. From that experience he draws ten lessons, from trust and empowerment to the claim that a leader's success is measured by how the team performs in his absence. The move is to treat his own constant availability as a control habit rather than a necessity. The most distinctive argument is that delegation must transfer authority and not merely tasks. The post is a first-person reflection with short framework pointers at the end of each lesson.
points: Constant availability and quick responses may reflect the leader's need for control more than real necessity, so stepping back is a test of the team's readiness.
Delegating tasks without decision authority keeps the purse strings tight and forces people to come back for every spend.
Clear decision processes, ownership and accountability let operations continue smoothly without oversight.
Deliberately creating space for others to lead surfaces hidden talent and builds the leadership pipeline.
The measure of a leader is how well the team performs when the leader is absent.
quotes: I was greeted by a team that had not just maintained the status quo but had thrived in my absence. Projects were on track, decisions had been made confidently, and any issues that had arisen were handled efficiently.
I realized that my constant availability, quick responses, and frequent check-ins might have been more about my own need for control than actual necessity.
If you only delegate tasks, you are giving them a budget to spend while keeping the purse strings tight and expecting them to come to you for every spend. And we all know how suffocating that can be.
Lesson: Effective delegation involves transferring not just tasks, but also the authority to make decisions related to those tasks.
My absence created opportunities for team members to step up and showcase their leadership skills and their initiative, which may otherwise have gone unnoticed.
true leadership isn’t about making yourself indispensable. It’s about developing a team that can function effectively, with or without you.
As a leader, sometimes the best gift you can give your team is to step back, trust them, and let them shine.
